SUTR-012 — SuperUnicode Cuneiform Sign Lists (SUCSL)

The binary-mapped Cuneiform sign schema, the compiled sign hierarchy, the zero-allocation O(1) sign, compound and sequence lookup engine, and the native extension model for custom epigraphic sign lists across the Cuneiform, Cuneiform Numbers and Punctuation, and Early Dynastic Cuneiform blocks of the Bridge plane

Standard ID: SUTR-012
Status: 1.0.0 — Published
Scope: The binary-mapped Cuneiform sign schema, the compiled sign hierarchy, the zero-allocation O(1) sign, compound and sequence lookup engine, and the native extension model for custom epigraphic sign lists across the Cuneiform, Cuneiform Numbers and Punctuation, and Early Dynastic Cuneiform blocks of the Bridge plane
Applies to: SUAS-012 (SUCD), SUAS-005 (SSP), SUTR-0 (SUCS Core), SUTR-1 (SUTF), SUTR-6 (Bridge), SUTR-10 (SUCM), SUTR-11 (SUMS), the SUF vector font engine, and every cuneiform text, corpus and rendering consumer
Last updated: 2026-10-22
Source: docs/sutr/SUTR-012-sucsl.md — this page is generated from it, and the repository copy governs where they differ.

1. Overview

Where UTR #56 Unicode Cuneiform Sign Lists documents how the Cuneiform blocks of the Unicode Standard were assembled — the sign lists, the values, the compound signs, the numerical notation and the ligature conventions — and leaves the mapping of a particular sign to a particular value to prose, a text-based catalog parser or an application-specific table, SUTR-012 (SUCSL) establishes the equivalent contract for SuperUnicode: the binary-mapped Cuneiform sign schema, the packed sign record, the compound composition pointer and the zero-allocation O(1) resolution engine that every SuperUnicode consumer uses instead of a runtime catalog.

SUCSL is a modular technical-report specification, a peer of SUTR-11 (SUMS) and SUTS-008 (SUSCH). It is the cuneiform member of the same family:

Report Counterpart Domain Compiled surface
SUTR-11 (SUMS) UTR #54 Mongolian shaping 12-byte shaping record, FVS table
SUTS-008 (SUSCH) UTS #39 Source-code safety Identifier profile, confusable table
SUTR-012 (SUCSL) UTR #56 Cuneiform sign lists 12-byte sign record, compound and sequence tables

The report is normative for the record layout, the flag vocabulary, the hash function, the lookup contract and the degradation rules. It is informative for the contents of the curated registry: the signs, values, wedge counts and period tags are version data compiled from the SUCD manifests and may grow without changing the engine.

1.1 Relation to UTR #56

UTR #56 is a Unicode Technical Report, not a UAX. It does not define new characters and it does not add normative properties to the code charts. It records how the Cuneiform repertoire was selected and how the sign lists were built, so that implementations can recover the intent behind a code chart whose glyphs are only representative. It covers three areas:

  1. The principles of Cuneiform encoding: signs, values, sequences, mergers and splits, representative glyphs, sign names and ligatures.
  2. The sign lists themselves: the Oracc Sign List ([OSL]) and the older Assyrian Sign List ([ASL]), their machine-readable form, and the signs that were withdrawn.
  3. References to the epigraphic literature from which the repertoire derives.

SUCSL keeps those three areas but changes their implementation status. The principles become the normative schema of §2 and §4. The sign lists become the compiled registry of §8. The references become the provenance notes of §3. Nothing in the report depends on a runtime text file, a locale, a regular expression or a heap allocation.

1.2 Scope and terminology

The key words MUST, MUST NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT and MAY in this report are to be interpreted as described in RFC 2119.

A sign is an abstract Cuneiform character with a stable codepoint. A value is a reading or meaning conventionally assigned to that sign: a Sumerian logogram, an Akkadian syllable, a Hittite reading, a numeral. A sign is polyvalent when it has more than one value. A compound sign is a sign whose structure is written as one sign built from other signs, such as GUD×KUR. A sequence is a sign that the encoding represents as an ordered list of other signs rather than as one atomic codepoint, such as GEME₂ = SAL.KUR. A merger is a historical process in which two signs become one; a split is the reverse.

The unit of the engine is one 31-bit SuperUnicode codepoint. SUTR-0 (SUCS Core) defines the three-space layout and the Sentinel. SUTR-1 (SUTF) defines the transport forms. SUCSL defines only what a Cuneiform codepoint means to a sign consumer.

1.3 Key architectural concepts

#### 1.3.1 Pre-compiled binary sign hierarchies

A traditional implementation parses a sign-list file, builds a dictionary of sign names to codepoints, and resolves a value by searching strings at run time. SUCSL replaces the dictionary with a static array of fixed-size records sorted by codepoint, plus an open-addressing index built once. A codepoint is the key; the record is the value. There is no string comparison on the hot path, and there is no per-query allocation.

The hierarchies are:

  • Codepoint → record. The 12-byte sucsl_sign_entry_t of §4.2.
  • Compound codepoint → components. The 24-byte sucsl_compound_t of §4.6.
  • Sequence name hash → components. The same descriptor with sign == 0.
  • Registry ordinal → record. The 1-based hierarchy index of §4.8.

#### 1.3.2 The four functional categories

Every curated sign is classified into one or more of four functional classes: Numerical, Syllabic, Logographic and Composite. The classes are packed into the sign_flags word of §4.3. They are not mutually exclusive in the data, because a sign such as AM is at once a logogram, a syllabogram and a structural compound. A single-category projection is provided for consumers that need one label; its precedence is normative and is stated in §4.3.

#### 1.3.3 Values are hashes, not strings

The engine stores a 32-bit FNV-1a hash of the sign's primary value skeleton, not the value string. This keeps the record at 12 bytes and keeps the module freestanding. The hash is an index and a hint, not an identity: two different values may collide, and the engine never treats a hash match as proof that two values are equal. Identity is carried by the codepoint. A consumer that needs the spelling reads it from the SUCD manifest, not from SUCSL. §4.4 states the normalization rules that make the hash reproducible.

#### 1.3.4 Compounds and sequences are separate tables

An atomic compound sign has a codepoint and a decomposition. A pure sequence has no atomic codepoint; it is a spelling convention for a sign that the encoding represents with two or three existing signs. Mixing the two in one namespace would make sign == 0 ambiguous and would force a linear scan. SUCSL therefore keeps sucsl_compounds[] (non-zero key, binary search by codepoint) and sucsl_sequences[] (zero key, binary search by name hash) separate. §4.6 specifies both.

#### 1.3.5 The RNUR extension

The Native & Neography Plane of SUAS-005 (SSP) reserves 0x00160000–0x0016FFFF for user-defined writing systems. SUCSL treats that range as a first-class extension space: an uncurated RNUR codepoint receives a synthesized record with the SUCSL_FLAG_EXTENSION bit, and a user-space toolchain may overlay its own sign table using the same binary layout. No kernel patch and no new codepoint assignment are required. §5 specifies the range and the set numbering.

1.4 The Cuneiform specification matrix

Concern UTR #56 treatment SUCSL treatment Section

Functional class Prose description Four packed flags + projection §4.3
Value Value list in prose FNV-1a hash of an ASCII skeleton §4.4
Compound sign "X times Y" name Component pointer table §4.6
Sequence "written as A.B" Name-hash sequence table §4.6
Numeral Numerical sign charts NUMERICAL + VARIANT flags §2.1.2
Period Glyph commentary 8-bit period tag §4.5
Rendering hint Representative glyph Wedge count byte §4.5

1.5 Cross-references

Specification Relationship
SUTR-0 (SUCS Core) Defines the 31-bit codepoint, the three spaces and the Sentinel.
SUTR-1 (SUTF) Defines the transport forms that carry a Cuneiform codepoint.
SUTR-6 (Bridge) Allocates the Cuneiform blocks inside the Bridge plane.

1.6 Why SUCSL is a modular SUTR

Ancient-script support is not a bootstrapping requirement of a microkernel. An image that never renders or indexes cuneiform text should not carry 3 KiB of sign tables. SUCSL is therefore a modular report: its engine is self-contained, its tables are static, and its omission does not affect any other specification. A kernel that includes it gets the O(1) contract; a kernel that omits it remains conformant to SUCS Core, SUTF and the Bridge, and simply does not resolve Cuneiform signs.

The module boundary is the header sutr/sutr_sucsl.h. It includes only <stdint.h>, <stdbool.h> and <stddef.h>, and it compiles under -ffreestanding -nostdlib.

2. Principles of Cuneiform Encoding

2.1 Cuneiform signs

A Cuneiform sign is a conventional arrangement of wedges impressed into clay. The encoding does not preserve the impression; it preserves the abstract sign, exactly as a Latin encoding preserves the letter and not the typeface. The code chart shows one representative glyph per sign, usually a Neo-Assyrian or Old Babylonian form chosen for legibility. That glyph is not normative and is not the only correct rendering (§2.4).

A sign acquires its values from the scribal tradition. The same sign can be a Sumerian word, an Akkadian syllable, a Hittite gloss and a numeral, sometimes in the same document. SUCSL records one primary value per curated sign and marks the functional classes; it does not attempt to enumerate every reading. The complete reading list belongs to the SUCD manifest, which is a text resource and is not compiled into the kernel.

#### 2.1.1 Transliteration

Transliteration is the ASCII representation of a sign sequence used by assyriologists and by the OSL. SUCSL defines a value skeleton so that a 32-bit hash is reproducible across tools and releases. The normalization rules are:

Input convention Skeleton rule Example
Lowercase or uppercase Fold to lowercase ASCII AM → am
Diacritics (š, ḫ, ṭ, ṣ, ū, ā) Fold to the ASCII digraph or base letter meš → mesh, ḫu → hu
Homophone subscript (₂, ₃, …) Append the ASCII digit u₂ → u2
Variant marker @v Drop the marker and its argument a@v → a
Compound multiplication (×) Replace with ASCII x GUD×KUR → gudxkur
Sequence separator (.) Replace with ASCII - SAL.KUR → sal-kur
Numeric subscript in a name Preserve the digit GAR₃ → gar3
Whitespace and punctuation Remove, except the separator NE ŠEŠIG → nesheshig

The skeleton is a hash key, not a display form. A user interface continues to show GUD×KUR, meš and u₂; only the hash sees gudxkur, mes and u2. The @v rule deserves emphasis: when a transliteration offers an alternative reading, the alternative does not create a second sign. It selects the same primary value and is recorded as a variant through SUCSL_FLAG_VARIANT or as a sequence descriptor. This is why the variant forms of the numerals in §2.1.2 share a value skeleton with their plain counterparts but carry a different codepoint and the VARIANT bit.

The "diš-less" notation follows from the same discipline. The numeral 1 is written diš, but a lone vertical wedge is frequently omitted in transliteration when the context makes the quantity clear. The skeleton of the bare numeral is therefore dish, not 1dish; a consumer that wants the quantity reads the codepoint, not the spelling.

#### 2.1.2 Numerals and stacking patterns

Cuneiform numerals are a separate repertoire. The Cuneiform Numbers and Punctuation block (U+12400–U+1247F) contains precomposed numeric signs for the common quantities, while the main block contains the wedge signs from which larger numbers are stacked. The important cases are:

Concept Plain form Variant form Encoding note
One DIŠ U+12079 — A lone wedge; often omitted in transliteration
One (AŠ) AŠ U+12038 — Also a syllabic sign; dil in some lists
Ten U U+1230B — One wedge, ten-value
Twenty U U U+12399 — Two stacked tens; Early Dynastic graphic
Thirty U U U U+1230D — Three stacked tens
Three 3(diš) U+12408 — Three vertical wedges
Four 4(diš) U+12409 4(limmu) U+1243C Ur III vs Neo-Assyrian graphic
Five 5(diš) U+1240A 5(aš) U+12403 Different wedge families
Seven 7(diš) U+1240C 7(imin) U+12441 / U+12442 Two variant traditions
Eight 8(diš) U+1240D 8(ussu) U+12444 / U+12445 Two variant traditions
Nine 9(diš) U+1240E 9(ilimmu) U+12446 / U+12447 Two variant traditions

The stacking pattern is the rule that a numeral is built by repeating a wedge a fixed number of times. It is not a font feature: the precomposed codepoint already names the quantity. U+12409 (four-diš) and U+1243C (four-limmu) are not interchangeable glyph variants of one abstract character; they are two encoded characters with different histories. SUCSL preserves the distinction through two different records, both NUMERICAL, one additionally VARIANT, and both tagged with their period. A consumer that normalizes them would destroy exactly the evidence an epigrapher needs.

U+12399 (U U) is the twenty-graphic; U+12409 is four-diš. They are in different blocks and were encoded for different reasons. The report calls out the pair because a naive "repeat the wedge" renderer can mistake one for the other when it ignores the block boundary. SUCSL's block predicate (§4.1) prevents that mistake at the API boundary.

2.2 Sequences

Some signs have no atomic codepoint. The encoding represents them as an ordered sequence of existing signs, and the sequence is the identity. The canonical examples are:

Sign Sequence Codepoints Meaning
GEME₂ SAL.KUR U+122A9 U+121B3 female servant
DIRI SI.A U+122DB U+12000 to be more, to exceed
IDIGNA GU₂.GAR₃ U+12118 U+120FC the Tigris
DALLA MAŠ.GU₂.GAR₃ U+12226 U+12118 U+120FC a type of sprout
U₅ ḪU.SI U+12137 U+122DB a bird; a ligature
Aššur AŠ.ŠUR U+12038 U+122E9 the god and the city
SIKI.LAM SIK₂.LAM U+122E0 U+121F4 wool
me-eš ME.EŠ₂ U+12228 U+120A0 the sequence spelling of meš

A sequence is not a canonical decomposition of an atomic sign. GEME₂ is not "the character SAL followed by the character KUR" in the way a Latin base plus combining mark is a decomposition; it is a spelling convention whose referent is a single lexical item. SUCSL therefore does not apply normalization to it. The sequence is emitted as written, and the sucsl_sequences[] row tells a consumer that the two signs form the named item.

2.3 Mergers and splits

The cuneiform repertoire is the product of three thousand years of scribal change. Signs merge, split, and change value. The encoding freezes one moment of that process, but the sign list must remember the others. SUCSL captures the history in three places: the primary value hash, the period tag, and the VARIANT flag.

The signs ŠAR₂ (U+122B9), ḪI (U+1212D), TI₂ (U+12397) and DIN (U+12077) are standard examples. Each has a reference glyph that is characteristic of a particular period — ŠAR₂ of the Early Dynastic corpus, TI₂ of the Old Assyrian tradition, DIN of the later tradition — while its value is attested across a wider span. A consumer that renders an Old Babylonian document with a Neo-Assyrian glyph is not making an encoding error, but it is making a historical one. The historical_period byte exists so that a font engine can select a style-appropriate glyph without re-parsing the document.

MEŠ (U+1238C) is an atomic sign. The spelling me-eš is a sequence of ME (U+12228) and EŠ₂ (U+120A0). They are not two spellings of one character: MEŠ is a single abstract sign, and me-eš is two signs whose combination a reader interprets as the same word. SUCSL stores MEŠ in sucsl_signs[] and me-eš in sucsl_sequences[], under different keys, so neither can be mistaken for the other. A text that uses the wrong one is a different text.

#### 2.3.1 Mergers and splits of sequences

The same distinction applies to ŠEŠ₂ (U+122C1) and SIKI.LAM (U+122E0 U+121F4). ŠEŠ₂ is an atomic sign; SIKI.LAM is a sequence. Their reference glyphs can resemble one another in some styles, and a careless transliteration can collapse them. SUCSL keeps the atomic sign in the sign table and the sequence in the sequence table; sutr_sucsl_is_sign() is true for the first and false for the second, and sutr_sucsl_find_sequence() is true for the second and false for the first.

Case Atomic codepoint Sequence key Distinguishing predicate
MEŠ vs me-eš U+1238C hash("me-esh") is_sign(0x1238C), no sequence hash("mesh")
ŠEŠ₂ vs SIKI.LAM U+122C1 hash("siki-lam") is_sign(0x122C1), sequence has two components
DIRI vs SI.A none hash("diri") is_sign(0x122DB) && is_sign(0x12000)
GEME₂ vs SAL.KUR none hash("geme2") is_sign(0x122A9) && is_sign(0x121B3)

The general rule is: if the encoding gives the sign an atomic codepoint, it is a sign; if it does not, it is a sequence. SUCSL never invents an atomic codepoint for a sequence and never decomposes an atomic sign into a sequence. This is the single most important invariant of the module, and §8.3 tests it directly.

2.4 Representative glyphs

The glyph in a code chart is a representative. It is usually chosen for legibility and for continuity with the sign list, not because it is the only attested form. The same sign may be written horizontally or vertically, with more or fewer wedges, and with different proportions in different periods. The encoding is not the glyph.

SUCSL exposes two rendering hints and no glyph data:

  • wedge_count — the number of constituent wedges in the reference form. It is a hint for a font engine that selects among pre-designed glyphs; it is not a constraint on the rendering. A value of zero means "unknown".
  • historical_period — the chronological tag of the reference form. A font engine may use it to choose an Early Dynastic, Ur III, Old Babylonian, Old Assyrian, Middle Assyrian, Neo-Assyrian or Hellenistic style.

The actual outlines belong to the SUF vector font engine. SUCSL does not embed an outline, a bitmap or a variation axis. This separation is deliberate: a kernel image may need to index signs without carrying a font, and a font may be updated without rebuilding the sign registry.

2.5 Sign names

A Unicode character name is an algorithmic identifier, not a value. The name CUNEIFORM SIGN GUD TIMES KUR records the structure of the sign: GUD combined with KUR. It does not say that the sign is read am, and it does not say that am is the only reading. The name is stable across releases; the value is a scholarly interpretation.

SUCSL preserves the structural name as a name hash in the compound and sequence descriptors. The skeleton rule is the same as §2.1.1, with one addition: the word TIMES becomes x. A sign whose name records a wedge modification rather than a multiplication, such as NE SHESHIG, has no x component; its conventional value bil2 is the key. Thus:

Unicode name Structural skeleton Hash
CUNEIFORM SIGN GUD TIMES KUR gudxkur 0xCB74D2C5
CUNEIFORM SIGN DUB TIMES ESH2 dubxesh2 0xAF07276A
CUNEIFORM SIGN GUM TIMES SHE gumxshe 0x80FA16FE
CUNEIFORM SIGN DUB TIMES SHE dubxshe 0x36817CDA
CUNEIFORM SIGN NE SHESHIG bil2 0x714E5A9E

The last row shows the exception: a sign whose name records a modification rather than a multiplication has no x component, and its conventional value bil2 is the key. The table is explicit, so the exception never has to be guessed at run time.

2.6 Ligatures

A ligature is a single glyph that represents a sequence of signs. It is a rendering choice, not an encoding. The sequence remains the encoded representation. The canonical cases are:

Ligature Sequence Codepoints Notes
U₅ ḪU.SI U+12137 U+122DB bird; discretionary in most styles
DIRI SI.A U+122DB U+12000 the sequence is the identity
Aššur AŠ.ŠUR U+12038 U+122E9 theophoric and toponymic
um-me UM.ME U+1231D U+12228 scholarly convention
nenni NE.NE U+12248 U+12248 conventional ligature

A sequence row carries SUCSL_COMPOUND_LIGATURE when the conventional rendering joins the components. The flag is a hint to the font engine; it is not a requirement. A renderer that emits two separate glyphs is still correct.

#### 2.6.1 Discretionary ligatures

A discretionary ligature is one that a font MAY apply and a text MAY forbid. SuperUnicode has no separate control codepoint for cuneiform ligatures. The format controls ZWNJ (U+200C) and ZWJ (U+200D) retain their general meaning: ZWNJ requests that the adjacent signs not be joined, and ZWJ requests that they be treated as a unit. Neither control is part of the Cuneiform blocks, and neither is stored in a sucsl_sign_entry_t.

The recommended model is:

  1. The encoded text contains the component signs in order.
  2. A sequence descriptor with the LIGATURE flag announces that a conventional joined glyph exists.
  3. The font engine applies the ligature unless a ZWNJ intervenes.
  4. A ZWJ may force the joined form where the font would otherwise break it.

Because the ligature is discretionary, two conformant renderers may produce different glyphs for the same sequence. They do not disagree about the text. SUCSL's job is to tell them that the sequence is a known one, not to force a particular outline.

2.7 Early Dynastic Cuneiform

The Early Dynastic Cuneiform block (U+12480–U+1254F) contains signs from the third millennium BCE that are not simply older drawings of the main-block signs. Some are distinct abstract characters with their own codepoints. SUCSL curates a representative set — AB×NUN TENU (U+12480), DIM×IGI (U+1248A) and LAK-648×SHESH+KI (U+12514) — and tags each with the Early Dynastic period. The block predicate of §4.1 includes it, so an uncurated Early Dynastic sign still receives a synthesized record rather than a rejection.

The Early Dynastic block is also where the LAK sign numbering of the sign lists is most visible. A LAK-648 name is a sign-list index, not a value; SUCSL stores it as the structural skeleton lak648 and leaves the value hash to the manifest. This is the same treatment as any other structural name.

3. The Oracc Sign List

3.1 [OSL] and [ASL]

The Oracc Sign List ([OSL]) is the modern machine-readable sign list maintained by the Open Richly Annotated Cuneiform Corpus. It assigns each sign a name, a Unicode encoding, a list of values and a set of notes. The older Assyrian Sign List ([ASL]) remains useful as a concordance: its numbering appears in the epigraphic literature long before Unicode, and many publications cite it. The two lists do not always agree on the boundaries of a sign, which is precisely why an implementation needs a compiled, versioned snapshot rather than a runtime guess.

SUCSL does not replace either list. It defines the binary form into which a conforming toolchain compiles one. The lists remain the scholarly authority for which signs exist and what they mean; SUCSL is the authority for how a compiled sign is represented and resolved.

3.2 The compiled manifest

The build pipeline is:

  1. Import. SUCD reads the OSL and ASL manifests and records every sign it can map to a SuperUnicode codepoint.
  2. Normalize. Each value and structural name is reduced to the skeleton of §2.1.1, and the FNV-1a hash is computed.
  3. Curate. A human reviewer resolves conflicts, assigns the primary value, the functional flags, the wedge count and the period tag, and marks withdrawn signs.
  4. Emit. The compiler writes sucsl_signs[], sucsl_compounds[] and sucsl_sequences[] in strictly ascending order, together with the compile-time geometry asserts.
  5. Verify. A reproducibility check recomputes every hash and every sort order before the image is linked.

The kernel never performs steps 1–5. It links the result. A release that adds a sign is a data change; the engine and the ABI are unchanged. This is the same division of labour that SUTR-11 uses for Mongolian and SUTS-008 uses for source-code confusables.

The following table maps an OSL record onto the compiled fields:

OSL field SUCSL field Transformation
Unicode codepoint codepoint Copied verbatim; must be in a Cuneiform block
Primary value primary_value_hash Skeleton, then FNV-1a
Sign class sign_flags Mapped to the four functional bits
Sign name sucsl_compound_t.name_hash Structural skeleton, then FNV-1a
Wedge count wedge_count Copied, clamped to 0–255
Period note historical_period Mapped to the eight period tags
Deprecation note SUCSL_FLAG_DEPRECATED Set when the OSL withdraws the sign
Variant note SUCSL_FLAG_VARIANT Set for an alternate stacking tradition

3.3 Deprecated signs

A deprecated sign is one that the standardized list has withdrawn. It is not deleted from the encoding, because legacy corpora contain it and a text that used it is still a text. SUCSL retains the record and sets SUCSL_FLAG_DEPRECATED. A conforming producer MUST NOT emit a deprecated sign in new text; a conforming consumer MUST still resolve one that it receives.

The three signs called out by UTR #56 are curated. The explanatory notes in the sign lists differ; SUCSL preserves the flag and leaves the prose to the SUCD manifest.

Sign Codepoint Status Reason
DUB×EŠ₂ U+1207F Deprecated Withdrawn; retained for legacy text
DUB×ŠE U+12376 Deprecated Withdrawn; retained for legacy text
GUM×ŠE U+12124 Deprecated Withdrawn; retained for legacy text

The records remain in sucsl_signs[] with their flags, and their compound decompositions remain in sucsl_compounds[] with SUCSL_COMPOUND_DEPRECATED. This is important for corpus migration: a tool can detect a deprecated sign, report its codepoint, and propose the replacement without a string search and without a separate exception table.

3.4 Correspondence to SUCSL records

Sign-list question SUCSL answer
Does this codepoint have a curated record? sutr_sucsl_is_sign(cp)
What is its function? sutr_sucsl_sign_category(cp) and the flag predicates
What is its primary value? sutr_sucsl_primary_value_hash(cp)
How many wedges in the reference form? sutr_sucsl_wedge_count(cp)
Which period is the reference form from? sutr_sucsl_historical_period(cp)
What is its sign-list ordinal? sutr_sucsl_sign_index(cp)
What are its components? sutr_sucsl_get_composition(cp, &c)
Is this spelling a sequence? sutr_sucsl_find_sequence(hash, &c)
Is the sign withdrawn? sutr_sucsl_is_deprecated(cp)

4. The SUCSL Schema

4.1 Zones and blocks

SUCSL reuses the zone taxonomy of SUTR-11 (SUMS) and SUAS-005 (SSP). A Cuneiform sign lives in the Bridge plane; the SCP is text space but carries no sign; the RNUR is the extension space; the Native plane carries native objects; the Trap, Sentinel and ExtSUCS zones are not text space.

Zone Range SUCSL behavior
Bridge 0x00000000–0x0010FFFF Cuneiform blocks are sign space; other values are not
SCP 0x00110000–0x0011FFFF Text space, no sign; NOT_CUNEIFORM
RNUR 0x00160000–0x0016FFFF Extension sign space; synthesized record
Native rest of 0x00120000–0x7FFFFFEF Native object, no sign; NOT_CUNEIFORM
Trap 0x7FFFFFF0–0x7FFFFFFE ILLEGAL_ZONE
Sentinel 0x7FFFFFFF ILLEGAL_ZONE
ExtSUCS 0x80000000–0xFFFFFFFF Plugin space; ILLEGAL_ZONE

The three Cuneiform blocks are:

Block Range Size Curated examples
Cuneiform U+12000–U+123FF 922 codepoints A, AN, DIŠ, ME, GUD×KUR, DUB×EŠ₂
Cuneiform Numbers and Punctuation U+12400–U+1247F 128 codepoints 4(diš), 4(limmu), 7(imin), 1(ban₂)
Early Dynastic Cuneiform U+12480–U+1254F 208 codepoints AB×NUN TENU, DIM×IGI, LAK-648

The ranges are inclusive. U+123FF is a Cuneiform codepoint; U+12400 is a Numbers codepoint; the boundary is not a gap. U+12550 is outside all three blocks and is not a sign for SUCSL, even though it lies in the Bridge plane.

4.2 The sign record

The sign record is fixed-size, padding-free and byte-aligned. It is the structure the user sketch specifies, and it is the ABI:

Offset Field Type Size Meaning
0 codepoint uint32_t 4 Raw 31-bit SuperUnicode Cuneiform codepoint
4 primary_value_hash uint32_t 4 FNV-1a of the primary value skeleton
8 sign_flags uint16_t 2 Packed classification flags (§4.3)
10 wedge_count uint8_t 1 Constituent wedges in the reference form; 0 = unknown
11 historical_period uint8_t 1 Chronological tag (§4.5)

sizeof(sucsl_sign_entry_t) is exactly 12 bytes. The header publishes the structure; the implementation contains compile-time asserts for the size and for every offset, so a compiler that inserts padding fails the build rather than silently changing the ABI.

The curated table obeys four invariants:

  1. Every codepoint is in a Cuneiform block.
  2. The table is strictly ascending in codepoint.
  3. Every record has a non-zero primary_value_hash and a non-zero wedge_count.
  4. Every sign_flags value is a subset of SUCSL_FLAG_ASSIGNED_MASK.

The first invariant keeps is_sign() and is_cuneiform() consistent. The second makes the hierarchy index stable and the enumeration deterministic. The third prevents an uncurated row from masquerading as a curated one. The fourth keeps the flag word forward-compatible: bits 8–15 are reserved and MUST read as zero in a curated record.

4.3 Sign flags and categories

The four flags of the sketch occupy bits 0–3:

Flag Value Meaning
SUCSL_FLAG_LOGOGRAM 1U << 0 Functions as an independent word sign
SUCSL_FLAG_SYLLABIC 1U << 1 Functions as a phonetic syllable value
SUCSL_FLAG_NUMERICAL 1U << 2 Part of a numerical notation system
SUCSL_FLAG_COMPOSITE 1U << 3 Built from multiple wedge components

Four derived flags occupy bits 4–7:

Flag Value Meaning
SUCSL_FLAG_DEPRECATED 1U << 4 Withdrawn or erroneous sign (§3.3)
SUCSL_FLAG_SEQUENCE 1U << 5 Encoded as a sequence of signs (§2.2)
SUCSL_FLAG_VARIANT 1U << 6 Variant stacking or glyph family (§2.1.2)
SUCSL_FLAG_UNCLASSIFIED 1U << 7 Synthesized record with no curated flags

SUCSL_FLAG_ASSIGNED_MASK is 0x00FF. A synthesized RNUR record additionally carries SUCSL_FLAG_EXTENSION (1U << 8), which distinguishes a custom epigraphic sign from a Bridge sign. Bits 9–15 are reserved.

The flags overlap by design. AM (U+12120) is a logogram, a syllabogram and a composite; GUD (U+1211E) is a logogram and a syllabogram but not a composite. A consumer that needs the full classification reads the flags. A consumer that needs exactly one label uses the projection sutr_sucsl_category_of(flags), whose precedence is normative:

Precedence Condition Category
1 NUMERICAL set SUCSL_CATEGORY_NUMERICAL
2 SYLLABIC set SUCSL_CATEGORY_SYLLABIC
3 LOGOGRAM set SUCSL_CATEGORY_LOGOGRAPHIC
4 COMPOSITE set SUCSL_CATEGORY_COMPOSITE
5 otherwise SUCSL_CATEGORY_UNKNOWN

The order is chosen so that the function wins over the structure. AM is classified as Syllabic, not Composite, because a reader who asks "what is this sign doing in this text?" is usually asking about its reading. A sign whose only flag is COMPOSITE, such as DUB×ŠE (U+12376), projects to Composite because it has no functional class of its own.

4.4 Primary-value hashing

The primary value is hashed with FNV-1a 32-bit:

h = 2166136261u;
for each byte b of the ASCII skeleton:
h ^= b;
h *= 16777619u;

The constants are SUCSL_FNV_OFFSET_BASIS and SUCSL_FNV_PRIME. The function sutr_sucsl_hash_value(const char *skeleton) implements the loop without a libc dependency. A NULL pointer returns 0; the empty string returns the offset basis. Both behaviours are tested.

The skeleton rules are the table of §2.1.1. The important consequences are:

  • am and AM both hash to 0x4024F153.
  • a@v normalizes to a and hashes to 0xE40C292C, the same as a; the marker selects a variant reading without changing the primary key.
  • meš normalizes to mesh and hashes to 0xA100BEBC. The sequence me-eš normalizes to me-esh and hashes to 0xC53E2B7A. The two hashes are different because MEŠ (U+1238C) is atomic and me-eš is a sequence.
  • GUD×KUR and gudxkur both hash to 0xCB74D2C5.
  • GEME₂ and geme2 both hash to 0x0D95F4AB.
  • GUD×KUR and gudxkur both hash to 0xCB74D2C5.
  • GEME₂ and geme2 both hash to 0x0D95F4AB.

The hash is not a checksum of the complete reading list. It is a stable index of the primary value only. A sign with five readings has one primary value and four alternates that live in SUCD. A consumer MUST NOT infer the absence of a reading from a hash mismatch.

A 32-bit hash can collide. SUCSL therefore treats a hash as a filter, never as an identity. The codepoint is the identity; the hash is a fast pre-check for a dictionary keyed by value. If two curated signs share a value hash (a homophone), both records are correct; the engine does not merge them, and the hierarchy index distinguishes them. The curated table is checked for duplicate codepoints, not for duplicate hashes.

4.5 Wedge count and historical period

wedge_count is a rendering hint, not a spelling. It counts the constituent wedges in the reference form, from 1 to 9 in the curated set. A consumer MAY use it to choose among pre-designed glyphs, to estimate advance width, or to decide whether a ligature is plausible. A consumer MUST NOT reject a sign because its count is unexpected; the count is version data and may be revised when the reference glyph changes.

historical_period is one of nine tags:

Tag Value Period
SUCSL_PERIOD_UNKNOWN 0 No chronological classification
SUCSL_PERIOD_EARLY_DYNASTIC 1 Early Dynastic IIIa–IIIb
SUCSL_PERIOD_UR_III 2 Ur III
SUCSL_PERIOD_OLD_BABYLONIAN 3 Old Babylonian
SUCSL_PERIOD_OLD_ASSYRIAN 4 Old Assyrian
SUCSL_PERIOD_MIDDLE_ASSYRIAN 5 Middle Assyrian
SUCSL_PERIOD_NEO_ASSYRIAN 6 Neo-Assyrian
SUCSL_PERIOD_HELLENISTIC 7 Hellenistic
SUCSL_PERIOD_ALL 8 Attested across the whole record

The tag describes the reference form, not the sign's entire history. ŠAR₂ is tagged Early Dynastic because its reference glyph is Early Dynastic; its value is attested later as well. A synthesized record is always SUCSL_PERIOD_UNKNOWN; an unknown period is not evidence of an unknown sign.

4.6 Compound composition and sequences

The compound descriptor is 24 bytes:

Offset Field Type Size Meaning
0 sign uint32_t 4 Atomic compound codepoint, or 0 for a sequence
4 name_hash uint32_t 4 FNV-1a of the structural-name skeleton
8 component_a uint32_t 4 First component codepoint
12 component_b uint32_t 4 Second component, or 0
16 component_c uint32_t 4 Third component, or 0
20 component_count uint8_t 1 1–3
21 compound_flags uint8_t 1 SUCSL_COMPOUND_* bits
22 reserved uint16_t 2 Must be zero

The flags are:

Flag Value Meaning
SUCSL_COMPOUND_SEQUENCE 1U << 0 Text is the component sequence
SUCSL_COMPOUND_LIGATURE 1U << 1 A style-dependent font ligature exists
SUCSL_COMPOUND_DEPRECATED 1U << 2 Withdrawn or erroneous sign
SUCSL_COMPOUND_EARLY 1U << 3 Third-millennium-only analysis

SUCSL_COMPOUND_FLAG_MASK is 0x00FF.

The atomic compound table is keyed by sign and sorted strictly ascending. It contains only records whose sign is non-zero. The sequence table is keyed by name_hash and sorted strictly ascending; every row has sign == 0. The two tables are separate because their keys have different types and because a linear scan over a mixed table would make the sign == 0 case slow and ambiguous.

The invariants are:

  1. In sucsl_compounds[], every sign is a curated sign and carries SUCSL_FLAG_COMPOSITE.
  2. Every component_a is a curated sign; component_b is non-zero when component_count >= 2; component_c is non-zero when component_count == 3.
  3. In sucsl_sequences[], every row has sign == 0, a non-zero name_hash, the SEQUENCE flag, and two or three curated components.
  4. Both tables are strictly ascending in their key.
  5. reserved is zero in every row.

The lookup functions are:

  • sutr_sucsl_get_composition(sign, &c) — binary search in the compound table.
  • sutr_sucsl_find_sequence(name_hash, &c) — binary search in the sequence table.
  • sutr_sucsl_compound_at(i, &c) and sutr_sucsl_sequence_at(i, &c) — enumeration in table order.

A failed lookup leaves the output untouched and returns false; it does not zero the caller's structure. This matches the rest of the corpus and lets a caller distinguish "not found" from "found a zero record".

4.7 O(1) resolution

The sign lookup is an open-addressing hash table over the curated array. The index has SUCSL_SIGN_INDEX_SIZE (512) slots of { uint16_t entry; uint8_t used; }, and the table has at most SUCSL_SIGN_CAPACITY (160) records. The load factor is therefore below one half, and the index is strictly larger than the capacity, so a free slot always exists.

The algorithm is:

init:
clear the 512 slots
for i in 0 .. count-1:
slot = hash_codepoint(signs[i].codepoint) & 511
while slot is used: slot = (slot + 1) & 511
slot.entry = i; slot.used = 1
ready = 1

lookup(cp):
if not ready: init
slot = hash_codepoint(cp) & 511
repeat at most 512 times:
if slot is empty: return not found
if signs[slot.entry].codepoint == cp: return &signs[slot.entry]
slot = (slot + 1) & 511
return not found

hash_codepoint is FNV-1a over the four little-endian bytes of the codepoint. It is a different function from hash_value: one hashes a codepoint key, the other hashes an ASCII skeleton. Keeping them separate prevents a value hash from accidentally being used as a table slot.

The probe is bounded by the table size, not by the number of records, so the worst case is 512 comparisons and the expected case is one. The index is built lazily on the first query and is idempotent; a second call to sutr_sucsl_init_registry() returns immediately. The build is allocation-free and touches only static storage. A multithreaded application SHOULD call sutr_sucsl_init_registry() once during single-threaded start-up; after that, lookups are read-only and may run concurrently.

4.8 Hierarchy indices and enumeration

sutr_sucsl_sign_index(cp) returns the 1-based position of a curated sign in sucsl_signs[], or 0 when the codepoint is not curated. The index is the SUCSL analog of a sign-list number: it is stable for a given compiled table and is useful for compact references and for cross-checking a manifest. It is not a Unicode property and it is not stable across releases that insert a sign.

sutr_sucsl_sign_at(i, &e) enumerates the table in 0-based order. sutr_sucsl_sign_count() returns the number of curated records. The pair is consistent: for every i in [0, count), sign_at(i) succeeds and sign_index(sign_at(i).codepoint) == i + 1. The enumeration is deterministic because the table is sorted, and it is the supported way to walk the registry without knowing a codepoint.

5. The RNUR Extension

The Native & Neography User Range (RNUR) is the SuperUnicode carve-out for writing systems that are not yet part of the standard repertoire. SUAS-005 (SSP) places it at 0x00160000–0x0016FFFF, inside the Native plane but treated as text space. SUCSL uses the same range as its custom sign-list space.

The range is exactly 65,536 codepoints, divided into 256 sets of 256:

Property Value
Minimum 0x00160000 (SUCSL_RNUR_MIN)
Maximum 0x0016FFFF (SUCSL_RNUR_MAX)
Size 65,536 codepoints
Set size 256 codepoints (SUCSL_RNUR_SET_SIZE)
Set count 256
Set number (cp — SUCSL_RNUR_MIN) >> 8

sutr_sucsl_is_neography(cp) is true exactly inside the range. sutr_sucsl_neography_set(cp, &set) returns the set number, from 0 for 0x160000–0x1600FF to 255 for 0x16FF00–0x16FFFF. The function is O(1) and allocation-free. It returns false for a codepoint outside the range and for a NULL output pointer.

A sign in the RNUR has no standard value, no standard wedge count and no standard period. The engine therefore returns a synthesized record:

entry.codepoint = cp;
entry.primary_value_hash = 0u;
entry.sign_flags = SUCSL_FLAG_UNCLASSIFIED | SUCSL_FLAG_EXTENSION;
entry.wedge_count = 0u;
entry.historical_period = SUCSL_PERIOD_UNKNOWN;

The SUCSL_FLAG_EXTENSION bit is the marker that distinguishes a custom sign from an uncurated Bridge sign. A consumer that wants to reject custom signs can test it; a consumer that wants to accept them can treat the record as a stable identity and read the value from its own overlay.

The extension model is deliberately table-shaped, not parser-shaped. A user-space toolchain that defines a custom sign list compiles its own sucsl_signs[] with the same 12-byte record and the same hash discipline, and resolves its signs before consulting the kernel table. The kernel table remains the fallback. Because the layout is public and the index is keyed by codepoint, an overlay can be a second static array with the same lookup procedure; no kernel patch, no new system call and no codepoint assignment are required.

Constraints on an overlay:

  1. Every custom codepoint MUST lie in the RNUR.
  2. The overlay MUST NOT shadow a Bridge cuneiform codepoint.
  3. The overlay MUST use the same FNV-1a functions if it wants its hashes to be comparable with the kernel table.
  4. The overlay MUST preserve the 12-byte record layout if it is exposed across the module boundary.
  5. A custom sign MUST NOT be emitted into text that claims to be standard SuperUnicode text; it is an application-private extension.

The RNUR is not a dumping ground for unencoded signs. It is a versioned extension namespace with a fixed geometry, so two tools that agree on a set number can exchange records without a negotiation protocol.

6. Degradation and Synthesized Records

SUCSL never returns a partially filled record on failure and never writes to an output structure it does not own. The behavior is summarized below.

Input Example get_sign_entry out_error Record
Curated Cuneiform U+12120 true SUCSL_OK Curated
Uncurated Cuneiform U+12001 true SUCSL_OK Synthesized UNCLASSIFIED
Uncurated RNUR U+160000 true SUCSL_OK Synthesized UNCLASSIFIED + EXTENSION
SCP U+110000 false SUCSL_ERR_NOT_CUNEIFORM Untouched
Native U+120000 false SUCSL_ERR_NOT_CUNEIFORM Untouched
Trap U+7FFFFFF0 false SUCSL_ERR_ILLEGAL_ZONE Untouched
Sentinel U+7FFFFFFF false SUCSL_ERR_ILLEGAL_ZONE Untouched
ExtSUCS U+80000000 false SUCSL_ERR_ILLEGAL_ZONE Untouched
NULL record NULL false SUCSL_ERR_NULL_ARGUMENT Not applicable
NULL error pointer any normal result not written Per input

Three rules follow from the table:

  1. Uncurated is not unknown. A codepoint in an encoded Cuneiform block has a stable abstract identity even if the curated table has not reached it. The synthesized record lets a consumer carry it through a pipeline, report it, and round-trip it without inventing a value. is_sign() remains false, so a consumer can distinguish "encoded but not curated" from "curated".
  2. A zone error is a type error. The Trap, Sentinel and ExtSUCS zones are not text. Returning a synthesized record for them would make an illegal codepoint look like a rare sign. SUCSL rejects them with ILLEGAL_ZONE.
  3. A non-cuneiform character is not a sign. ASCII, Latin, Arabic, emoji and the SCP are text space but carry no cuneiform sign. They are rejected with NOT_CUNEIFORM, which is a weaker failure than ILLEGAL_ZONE and lets a caller distinguish "wrong character" from "corrupt codepoint".

The extended entry point sutr_sucsl_get_sign_entry_ex() reports the reason. The convenience wrapper sutr_sucsl_get_sign_entry() discards it. Both share one implementation, so they cannot drift. If out_error is NULL the function still works; if out_entry is NULL it returns false without dereferencing it.

A failed call leaves *out_entry exactly as the caller left it. This is normative: a caller may initialize a record once and reuse it across a loop, and a failure will not silently zero a field that the caller was about to inspect. The tests assert the post-condition for the NULL, zone and non-cuneiform cases.

7. Complexity, Memory and Conformance

7.1 Time and space

Operation Expected Worst case Allocation
sutr_sucsl_init_registry() O(n + 512), once O(n + 512) None
sutr_sucsl_get_sign_entry() O(1) O(512) probes None
sutr_sucsl_is_sign() and predicates O(1) O(512) probes None
sutr_sucsl_sign_index() O(1) O(512) probes None
sutr_sucsl_get_composition() O(log 5) O(log 5) None
sutr_sucsl_find_sequence() O(log 8) O(log 8) None
sutr_sucsl_sign_at() O(1) O(1) None
sutr_sucsl_hash_value() O(len) O(len) None
sutr_sucsl_zone_of() O(1) O(1) None

n is SUCSL_SIGN_COUNT, at most SUCSL_SIGN_CAPACITY (160). The probe bound is the index size (512), not n, so the worst case is a constant. The expected probe count at the current load factor (86/512 = 0.17) is close to one.

The static footprint is:

Object Size Notes
sucsl_signs[] 86 × 12 = 1,032 B Curated records
sucsl_compounds[] 5 × 24 = 120 B Atomic compounds
sucsl_sequences[] 8 × 24 = 192 B Sequence descriptors
sucsl_index[] 512 × 4 = 2,048 B { uint16_t; uint8_t; } with padding
Strings and helpers < 1 KiB Taxonomy names, version
Total ≈ 3.4 KiB Compile-time constant

The index slot is 4 bytes because the compiler pads the two-byte entry field and the one-byte used field to the alignment of uint16_t. The header does not expose the slot type, so the padding is an implementation detail; the compile-time assert SUCSL_SIGN_INDEX_SIZE > SUCSL_SIGN_CAPACITY is what guarantees that a free slot exists.

The module has no heap allocation, no malloc, no free, no realloc, no variable-length array, no recursion and no libc call. It includes only <stdint.h>, <stdbool.h> and <stddef.h>. It compiles under -ffreestanding -nostdlib and under -std=c99 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic without a diagnostic.

7.2 Normative requirements

A conforming implementation of SUCSL:

  • R1. MUST represent a codepoint as a 31-bit unsigned value and MUST reject the Sentinel and the ExtSUCS range with SUCSL_ERR_ILLEGAL_ZONE.
  • R2. MUST expose the 12-byte sucsl_sign_entry_t with the field offsets of §4.2, and MUST fail the build if the layout changes.
  • R3. MUST assign the four sketch flags the values 1, 2, 4, 8 and MUST keep bits 8–15 reserved except for SUCSL_FLAG_EXTENSION on RNUR records.
  • R4. MUST compute primary_value_hash with FNV-1a 32-bit over the ASCII skeleton of §2.1.1.
  • R5. MUST resolve a curated sign in expected O(1) time and MUST NOT scan the table linearly on the lookup path.
  • R6. MUST NOT allocate on the heap, use a variable-length array, or call a libc function on any code path.
  • R7. MUST synthesize a record for an uncurated Cuneiform or RNUR codepoint and MUST mark it UNCLASSIFIED (and EXTENSION for RNUR).
  • R8. MUST reject SCP, Native and non-cuneiform Bridge values with NOT_CUNEIFORM, and Trap/Sentinel/ExtSUCS with ILLEGAL_ZONE.
  • R9. MUST retain deprecated signs and mark them DEPRECATED; MUST NOT emit them in new text.
  • R10. MUST keep sucsl_signs[] strictly ascending in codepoint and the compound and sequence tables strictly ascending in their keys.
  • R11. MUST make sutr_sucsl_init_registry() idempotent and MUST NOT require a second call after the first query.
  • R12. MUST leave the output record untouched on every failure path.

A conforming producer additionally MUST NOT create an atomic codepoint for a sequence, MUST NOT decompose an atomic sign into a sequence, and MUST NOT use a deprecated sign in new text. A conforming consumer MUST accept a synthesized record, MUST preserve an unknown codepoint across a round trip, and MUST NOT infer a value from a hash collision.

7.3 Conformance tiers

SUCSL publishes the claim sucsl at SUCM tier L0 (see SUTR-10). L0 covers the deterministic, stateless subset: the record layout, the flags, the hash, the zone rules, the synthesized records, the deprecated records and the O(1) lookup. The higher tiers add corpus-scale behavior that is out of scope for a static table, such as a full OSL import, a font-driven glyph selection and a multi-table overlay. The claim is recorded in sutr_sucm with version 1.0.0 and the clause set SUCM_CLAUSES_L0.

The claim is a statement about this engine, not about the completeness of the curated data. A release that adds a sign changes the data version in SUCD, not the claim. A release that changes the record layout, the flag values, the hash or the degradation rules requires a new SUCSL minor or major version and a new claim.

8. Reference Implementation and Verification

The reference implementation lives in src/sutr/sutr_sucsl.c, the public surface in include/sutr/sutr_sucsl.h, and the unit tests in tests/test_sutr_sucsl.c. It is linked into sutr_static and is exercised by the test_sutr_sucsl CTest target, the unified smoke test and the SSRE registry test.

8.1 API summary

Function Purpose

sutr_sucsl_primary_value_hash(cp) Stored hash, or 0
sutr_sucsl_wedge_count(cp) Stored wedge count, or 0

sutr_sucsl_status_code_name(code) "SUCSL_OK", …

Every pointer output is optional only where the documentation says so. A NULL output pointer is a false return with SUCSL_ERR_NULL_ARGUMENT for the entry point, and a false return for the table accessors; it is never a crash.

8.2 Curated registry snapshot

Quantity Value
Curated signs 86
Logogram flag set 49
Syllabic flag set 50
Numerical flag set 31
Composite flag set 9
Deprecated flag set 3
Variant flag set 10
Atomic compounds 5
Sequences 8
First curated codepoint U+12000 (A)
Last curated codepoint U+12514 (LAK-648×SHESH+KI)
Index of U+12120 (GUD×KUR) 21

The flag counts overlap, so they do not sum to 86. A sign may be a logogram, a syllabogram and a composite at once. The category projection assigns exactly one of the five category values to each sign, and the sum of the five projected counts is 86.

The canonical value hashes are:

Skeleton Hash Identity
am 0x4024F153 GUD×KUR, U+12120
mes 0xD4AD6BBC MES, U+12229
mesh 0xA100BEBC MEŠ, U+1238C
me-esh 0xC53E2B7A ME.EŠ₂ sequence
gudxkur 0xCB74D2C5 GUD×KUR name
geme2 0x0D95F4AB SAL.KUR sequence
diri 0x635E3147 SI.A sequence
idigna 0x0D9D7CCD GU₂.GAR₃ sequence
dalla 0xB91EC5A5 MAŠ.GU₂.GAR₃ sequence
u5 0x0842AE3F ḪU.SI ligature
ash-shur 0x158520B6 AŠ.ŠUR ligature
siki-lam 0xD7AE3C7E SIK₂.LAM sequence
dubxesh2 0xAF07276A DUB×EŠ₂, U+1207F
gumxshe 0x80FA16FE GUM×ŠE, U+12124
dubxshe 0x36817CDA DUB×ŠE, U+12376

sutr_sucsl_hash_codepoint(0x12000) is 0x0269E40C; it is a key hash, not a value hash, and it is never compared with the table above.

8.3 Verification gates

A release of SUCSL passes:

  1. Standalone compile. `cc -std=c99 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Iinclude -c src/sutr/sutr_sucsl.c` with no diagnostic.
  2. Unit tests. test_sutr_sucsl covers 13 groups: version and geometry, zones, RNUR sets, hashing, curated resolution, predicates, periods, composition, sequences, enumeration, idempotent initialization, taxonomy and SSRE registration.
  3. Registry self-consistency. Every curated row is ascending, in a Cuneiform block, has a non-zero hash and wedge count, and round-trips through get_sign_entry and sign_index.
  4. Table self-consistency. Every compound row is a curated composite with curated components; every sequence row has sign == 0, two or three curated components, and a non-zero name hash; both tables are ascending.
  5. Unified smoke test. unified/test_unified.c includes the header and resolves AM, GUD×KUR, GEME₂, a numeral, a deprecated composite and an illegal zone alongside every other module.
  6. Registry tests. test_suas_ssre sees 38 specifications, 16 mandatory, 9 optional and 13 reference; test_sutr_sucm sees 32 engines and 32 claims and resolves the sucsl claim at L0.
  7. Documentation check. verify-docs accepts the report's field block, headings and cross-references, and the website generator emits the SUTR-012 page from this file.

The hash table is also checked by an independent generator that recomputes every FNV-1a value from the source skeletons and compares it with the compiled table; a mismatch fails the build before the image is linked.

Annex B — Worked Examples

B.1 Resolve a composite sign

#include "sutr/sutr_sucsl.h"

sucsl_sign_entry_t e;
sucsl_compound_t c;

sutr_sucsl_init_registry();
if (sutr_sucsl_get_sign_entry(0x12120u, &e)) {
/* AM = GUD x KUR */
/* e.sign_flags == LOGOGRAM | SYLLABIC | COMPOSITE */
/* e.primary_value_hash == 0x4024F153 */
/* e.wedge_count == 7 */
/* e.historical_period == SUCSL_PERIOD_ALL */
}
if (sutr_sucsl_get_composition(0x12120u, &c)) {
/* c.component_a == 0x1211E (GUD), c.component_b == 0x121B3 (KUR) */
/* c.component_count == 2, c.name_hash == 0xCB74D2C5 */
}

B.2 Distinguish four-diš from four-limmu

sucsl_sign_entry_t plain, variant;

sutr_sucsl_get_sign_entry(0x12409u, &plain); /* FOUR DISH */
sutr_sucsl_get_sign_entry(0x1243Cu, &variant); /* FOUR LIMMU */

/* plain.sign_flags == SUCSL_FLAG_NUMERICAL */
/* variant.sign_flags == SUCSL_FLAG_NUMERICAL | SUCSL_FLAG_VARIANT */
/* plain.historical_period == SUCSL_PERIOD_UR_III */
/* variant.historical_period == SUCSL_PERIOD_NEO_ASSYRIAN */

The two records are not normalizable into one another. A consumer that wants the quantity reads NUMERICAL; a consumer that wants the period reads historical_period.

B.3 Distinguish MEŠ from me-eš

sucsl_compound_t seq;

/* MEŠ is atomic. */
(void)sutr_sucsl_is_sign(0x1238Cu); /* true */

/* "me-eš" is a sequence. */
(void)sutr_sucsl_find_sequence(sutr_sucsl_hash_value("me-esh"), &seq);
/* seq.component_a == 0x12228 (ME), seq.component_b == 0x120A0 (EŠ₂) */

/* There is no sequence named "mesh"; the atomic sign owns that skeleton. */
(void)sutr_sucsl_find_sequence(sutr_sucsl_hash_value("mesh"), &seq); /* false */

B.4 Detect a deprecated sign

sucsl_sign_entry_t e;
sucsl_compound_t c;

sutr_sucsl_get_sign_entry(0x1207Fu, &e); /* DUB x EŠ₂ */
/* e.sign_flags & SUCSL_FLAG_DEPRECATED != 0 */

sutr_sucsl_get_composition(0x1207Fu, &c);
/* c.component_a == 0x1207E (DUB), c.component_b == 0x120A0 (EŠ₂) */
/* c.compound_flags & SUCSL_COMPOUND_DEPRECATED != 0 */

A producer should not emit U+1207F in new text. A consumer should still resolve it, report it, and offer the replacement from the manifest.

B.5 Accept a custom RNUR sign

sucsl_sign_entry_t e;
uint32_t set;

sutr_sucsl_get_sign_entry(0x160000u, &e);
/* e.sign_flags == SUCSL_FLAG_UNCLASSIFIED | SUCSL_FLAG_EXTENSION */
/* e.primary_value_hash == 0, e.historical_period == SUCSL_PERIOD_UNKNOWN */

sutr_sucsl_neography_set(0x160000u, &set); /* true, set == 0 */
sutr_sucsl_neography_set(0x160100u, &set); /* true, set == 1 */
sutr_sucsl_neography_set(0x12000u, &set); /* false */

The application overlay supplies the value, the wedge count and the period; the engine supplies the stable identity and the set arithmetic.

B.6 Reject a non-sign

sucsl_sign_entry_t e;
sucsl_status_code_t err;

/* Ordinary character: text space, no sign. */
(void)sutr_sucsl_get_sign_entry_ex(0x41u, &e, &err);
/* false, err == SUCSL_ERR_NOT_CUNEIFORM */

/* SCP: text space, no sign. */
(void)sutr_sucsl_get_sign_entry_ex(0x110000u, &e, &err);
/* false, err == SUCSL_ERR_NOT_CUNEIFORM */

/* Sentinel: not text space. */
(void)sutr_sucsl_get_sign_entry_ex(0x7FFFFFFFu, &e, &err);
/* false, err == SUCSL_ERR_ILLEGAL_ZONE */

A failure leaves e untouched. The test suite initializes the record to a sentinel value and asserts that the sentinel survives.

Annex C — Change Log

Version Date Change
1.0.0 2026-10-22 Initial publication. Publishes the 12-byte sign record, the four sketch flags and four derived flags, the FNV-1a value and key hashes, the compound and sequence descriptor, the O(1) open-addressing index, the zone and block taxonomy, the RNUR extension model, and the degradation rules. Ships 86 curated signs, 5 atomic compounds and 8 sequences. Registers sucsl in SUCM at tier L0 and adds SUTR-012 to SSRE.

The identifier SUTR-012 is the published module identifier and is intentionally zero-padded; it is the twelfth reference report. The zero-padded form is part of the ABI (SUCSL_SPEC_ID), so a consumer that compares the literal string must use the padded form.
